nameStory: The Common Dolphin gets its name from being the most abundant dolphin species in warm ocean waters worldwide. 'Dolphin' comes from the ancient Greek word 'delphis,' meaning 'womb,' referring to the mammal's live birth of young. Despite the name 'common,' seeing these playful marine mammals is anything but ordinary!
description: Common Dolphins are sleek, streamlined marine mammals known for their distinctive hourglass or crisscross color pattern along their sides. They typically measure 6-8 feet long and weigh between 150-300 pounds, with females usually being slightly smaller than males. Their most striking feature is the beautiful tan, yellow, or gray patches that create an hourglass shape on their flanks, contrasting sharply with their dark gray backs and white bellies. They have a prominent beak and a tall, curved dorsal fin that cuts gracefully through the water.

idTips.label: Color Pattern
idTips.description: Look for the distinctive hourglass or crisscross tan/yellow pattern on the sides - this creates a striking visual that looks like overlapping patches when the dolphin surfaces

idTips.label: Size & Shape
idTips.description: Medium-sized dolphins about 6-8 feet long with a sleek, torpedo-shaped body and prominent beak that's clearly defined from the rounded forehead

idTips.label: Dorsal Fin
idTips.description: Tall, curved dorsal fin that's dark gray to black and positioned in the center of the back - often the first thing you'll spot as they surface

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Highly social and acrobatic - often seen leaping completely out of the water, bow-riding boats, and traveling in large pods of dozens to hundreds of individuals

idTips.label: Swimming Pattern
idTips.description: Fast swimmers that create distinctive splashes when surfacing, often appearing to 'porpoise' through the water with rhythmic leaps

habitat: Common Dolphins prefer the deeper, offshore waters of the Atlantic Ocean beyond New England's continental shelf, typically in areas where water temperatures remain above 50°F. They're most often spotted during whale watching trips 20+ miles offshore, especially around underwater canyons and areas with strong currents that concentrate their fish prey. Look for them in the Gulf Stream's warm waters and areas where cold and warm currents mix.

seasonality.spring: Best viewing begins as waters warm, with dolphins following fish migrations closer to New England waters. Peak sighting opportunities start in May.
seasonality.summer: Prime season for spotting Common Dolphins on whale watching trips, as warm Gulf Stream waters bring both the dolphins and their prey closest to shore.
seasonality.fall: Still good viewing through October as dolphins remain in warmer offshore waters, though sightings become less predictable as they begin moving to winter areas.
seasonality.winter: Rare sightings as most dolphins move to warmer southern waters, though occasional individuals may be spotted during unusually warm winter periods.

funFact: Common Dolphins are nature's speed demons of the sea - they can swim up to 35 miles per hour and have been observed leaping over 20 feet out of the water, higher than a two-story building!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Atlantic White-sided Dolphins, but Common Dolphins have the distinctive tan/yellow hourglass pattern on their sides while White-sided Dolphins have bold white and yellow stripes. Remember: Common Dolphins have an 'hourglass figure' while White-sided Dolphins have racing stripes.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'common' can be misleading for New England waters - while they're the most abundant dolphin globally in warm waters, they're actually less frequently seen here than other species like Harbor Porpoises or Atlantic White-sided Dolphins due to their preference for warmer, offshore waters.
compareHints: Common Dolphins are the only species in their genus found in New England waters, making them unique among local dolphins. Compared to other New England dolphins, they're distinguished by their hourglass color pattern - no other local dolphin species has this distinctive tan and yellow marking that creates such a striking visual contrast against their gray and white coloring.
